7588339317: The Mechanics of Mortality Credits & Longevity Risk Pooling
4299660fde: A lifetime annuity pools longevity risk. Money left behind by annuitants who die earlier than average helps fund payments to those who live longer — the "mortality credit". That is why a life annuity can pay more each year than you could safely withdraw from the same savings on your own, where you'd have to plan for living to 95 or beyond.
1308030d7a: The trade-off: with a life-only contract, if you die early the remaining value stays in the pool. Guarantee periods and joint options reduce the payout in exchange for protecting heirs or a spouse.
18be5c15d5: Model used here: Gompertz mortality (modal age 90, dispersion 10 years) — roughly annuitant-level longevity. Real quotes also reflect sex, health, insurer expenses and current bond yields.
ac291f3752: Tax treatment depends on how the annuity was funded. Qualified annuities bought with pre-tax IRA or 401(k) money are generally taxed as ordinary income when paid out, and are subject to Required Minimum Distribution rules (RMDs start at 73, or 75 for people born in 1960 or later).
b794b5d164: Non-qualified annuities bought with after-tax savings use an exclusion ratio (IRC § 72): part of each payment is a tax-free return of your premium and part is taxable earnings, until your cost basis has been recovered.
6c960edf02: Sources: IRS Publication 575 (pension and annuity income) and Publication 939 (general rule for pensions and annuities).

2ed15257a4: How the lifetime income estimate works
0a5841d1bb: During deferral the premium grows at your assumed rate. At the payout age, the balance is converted to a monthly income by dividing it by an annuity factor: the present value, at the insurer pricing rate, of $1 a month paid for as long as the chosen option pays — weighted by the chance the annuitant (or either spouse) is still alive, with guaranteed months counted in full and COLA step-ups included. It's an estimate for comparing options, not an insurer quote.

e884dfca2d: Does trade-in value reduce sales tax?
c5bf083aa4: In most US states, yes — sales tax is calculated on the price after subtracting your trade-in value, not the full vehicle price.
fdc3d62ea5: Should I include destination or dealer fees?
e3a8d03c0a: Yes — enter them in the Dealer Fees, Title & Documentation field (or add them to the vehicle price). They're typically rolled into the loan, so leaving them out understates the amount financed.
6b52790189: Is it better to lease or finance a car?
ece04a0d49: Financing builds equity and has no mileage limits, while leasing typically offers lower monthly payments but no ownership at the end — the right choice depends on how long you keep vehicles and how much you drive.
7c8468b7c0: How much should my down payment be?
086d11ca06: 20% is a common guideline for new cars and 10% for used, though any amount that avoids being 'underwater' (owing more than the car's worth) as it depreciates is reasonable.
482d627fd9: Should I choose a shorter or longer auto loan term?
5c0c19efa7: Shorter terms (36-48 months) minimize total interest and reduce the risk of owing more than the car is worth, while longer terms lower the monthly payment at a higher total cost.
42290896e1: Is it worth negotiating the vehicle price separately from financing?
bffb53a9eb: Yes — negotiating price and financing separately, rather than focusing only on the monthly payment, generally leads to a better overall deal since dealers can adjust either variable to hit a target monthly number.
17f536e369: Does a manufacturer rebate lower my sales tax too?
c4afd053f1: It depends on your state. Most states tax the vehicle's full pre-rebate price, so a rebate lowers your loan amount but not your tax bill. A handful of states (including Arizona, Iowa, Kansas, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, Texas, and Wyoming) tax the post-rebate price instead.
